transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-03-12
Start time: 16:00 UTC
Duration: ~52 minutes
Location: Zoom
Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood SE), Priya Nair (ArgosPay CTO), Carlos Mendes (ArgosPay Head of Eng), Ava Thompson (ArgosPay Platform SRE)

Auto-generated summary (may be rough):
- Focus: prompt/prefix cache strategies for multi-tenant workloads, hit-rate improvement, cache key design, safety/isolation, and implications for batching/quantization and VPC/on-prem deployments.
- Outcome: agreed prototype plan to fingerprint prompts, namespace keys per-tenant, run targeted perf runs, and validate eviction/TTL policies in a private deployment.

Topics discussed:
- Prompt normalization and hashing strategies
- Per-tenant namespaces and collision risk
- Cache hit-rate metrics and observational signals
- Interaction with batching and KV cache warmup
- Quantization implications for cache determinism
- VPC/on-prem memory/security constraints and HSM/KMS integration

Action items (as recorded by fireflies, may be noisy):
- See metadata.action_items for assigned tasks

Transcript:
[00:00:00] Maya: all right everyone, thanks for joining. uh quick intros, i'm maya, AE at Redwood. Liam's our SE, he's gonna drive the technical bits. Priya, do you wanna intro the argospay folks?
[00:00:14] Priya: yep, hi all. i'm priya, cto at argospay. carlos is on for infra, ava is our platform sre. we've been seeing throughput spikes and curious about prefix caching to cut token costs.
[00:00:29] Carlos: hey. specifically, we've got multi-tenant traffic where a lot of prompts share common legal boilerplate, so we think prefix caching could help, but worried about cross-tenant leakage.
[00:00:41] Liam: yeah totally, that's the main tradeoff. We wanted to go over approaches for keying the cache, hit-rate expectations, and safe namespace strategies, and then touch on the VPC/on-prem constraints you mentioned.
[00:00:56] Maya: quick agenda, we'll review how redwood's KV prefix cache works at a high level, then dive into prompt fingerprinting, namespace patterns, collision risk, metrics to watch, and then ops concerns for private deployments.
[00:01:10] Priya: sounds good.

[00:01:30] Liam: ok starting with basics, our prefix cache stores per-sequence KV entries to accelerate autoregressive decoding. In practice we key entries by a fingerprint of the prompt prefix plus a model-version id and optionally a tenant id namespace. The fingerprint is typically a sha256 or murmurhash of a normalized prompt.
[00:01:58] Ava: when you say normalized, what steps are you doing? whitespace, punctuation?
[00:02:04] Liam: yes, normalization pipeline: strip leading/trailing whitespace, collapse repeated spaces, canonicalize unicode, optionally lowercasing for non-case-sensitive flows, and remove ephemeral metadata (timestamps, request ids) if it's predictable. But normalization is a double-edged sword — over-normalize and you might group prompts that shouldn't be cached together.
[00:02:27] Priya: hmm, for us, we have merchant-specific headers embedded in prompts for routing. we'd like those to be stripped for caching, but only if it doesn't affect output. any heuristics?
[00:02:38] Liam: common approach: define a prompt template where the variable slots are explicitly tokenized-out before hashing. So you produce a canonical 'template string' and a separate slot of variables. You hash the template. When you reconstruct the request you still include the variables in the generation step but reuse the cached KVs for the template.
[00:02:58] Carlos: and that requires application-side changes to send template identifiers?
[00:03:03] Liam: ideally yes. If you can send a template_id or pre-normalized prompt, hit rates improve and collision risk drops. If app changes aren't possible, you can run an automatic slotting heuristic, but it's brittle.

[00:03:30] [00:03:30] Speaker 4: mhm (unintelligible)
[00:03:35] Maya: on collision risk, what are the main failure modes we should watch for?
[00:03:39] Liam: collisions primarily come from hash space collisions (rare with sha256) or from over-aggressive normalization that merges semantically distinct prompts. Operationally the bigger risk is tenant namespace leakage: if you only key by prompt fingerprint and model id, two tenants with identical prompts could get served identical cached KVs, which may be fine for stateless prompts, but not when prompts include tenant-specific system messages or private data.
[00:04:04] Priya: ok so per-tenant namespace is basically mandatory for us?
[00:04:08] Liam: for the safest posture yes — include tenant_id as part of the cache key. We also support layered keys: [model_version, prompt_fingerprint, tenant_id] and we can optionally fall back to a shared namespace for low-sensitivity templates if you want to reduce duplication.
[00:04:24] Ava: how does that impact memory footprint? we have a limited GPU memory budget on our on-prem nodes.
[00:04:30] Liam: it increases total unique key space; more namespaces == more cached entries. Two mitigations: 1) TTL and frequency-based eviction — don't keep cold entries forever; 2) shared prefix cache with explicit per-tenant access control: keep a small global cache for common templates and a per-tenant hot slab. In private deployments you can tune slab sizes.

[00:04:57] Carlos: can you explain the slab model a bit?
[00:05:00] Liam: sure. think of the cache memory partitioned: a global slab (e.g., 30% of KV store) for shared, high-hit templates, and per-tenant slabs split across remaining memory. If a tenant's slab grows beyond quota, its least-recently-used entries are evicted first. This prevents noisy neighbors from exhausting memory.

[00:05:21] [00:05:21] Carlos: might we see performance cliffs if a tenant has a spike?
[00:05:24] Liam: yes if no proper throttles. Redwood can enforce request rate limits and backpressure into batching so a single tenant can't saturate GPU cache replicas. Also automatic fallback to lower-SLA hosted variants or reduced batch sizes is supported.

[00:05:45] Priya: on hit-rate expectations, what should we plan for? we measured some quick runs and saw 12-18% hit rate on raw prompts.
[00:05:53] Liam: that depends on workload. With template extraction and normalization you can often move to 40-60% for UI-style prompts where the prefix is identical. For transactional and highly customized prompts fewer matches. The metric you want to optimize for is token-saved-per-request and latency improvement, not purely hit-rate. A low hit rate on long prefixes can still save many decoder steps.
[00:06:17] Maya: we should also instrument prefix similarity: we provide a breakdown in the console that shows most-common prompt templates and their cohort frequencies. That helps prioritize which templates to template-ize.

[00:06:30] Ava: how deterministic is caching when models are quantized? we use int8 quantization in some on-prem nodes.
[00:06:36] Liam: quantization doesn't change keying — keys are computed from prompts and model_version identifiers. But quantization can affect generation determinism slightly which might affect downstream evaluation if you're relying on exact token matches. For KV cache correctness, the runtime must ensure that the cached intermediate representations are compatible with the execution kernel. Redwood's runtime stores model-variant identifiers including quantization profile; the cache key includes that profile so incompatible entries won't be used.
[00:07:02] Priya: so if we retrain or change quantization, those are different cache namespaces?
[00:07:06] Liam: yes, model-version + quant-profile are included. Seamless rollout requires warming the cache on the new variant or using canary routing until warm.

[00:07:20] [00:07:20] Carlos: what about security: is there any chance KV entries contain PII or tenant secrets?
[00:07:26] Liam: KV entries are intermediate activations, generally not plain-text, but as a conservative control we recommend application-level removal of secrets from prompt prefixes and per-tenant namespaces plus encryption at rest. In private deployments, KV stores can be encrypted using your KMS and access restricted to tenant-scoped runtime processes.
[00:07:47] Priya: good. we need to document that for compliance (SOC2 section).

[00:07:55] Maya: quick question on key derivation: do you ever salt hashes with nonces or rotate salts?
[00:08:01] Liam: you can salt at two levels. For tenant isolation, tenant_id acts as an implicit salt. For extra security, especially in multi-tenant hosted contexts, we support a per-deployment salt that is rotated monthly; when salt rotates old entries are invalidated. Salt rotation is a blunt instrument — it flushes cache but can be part of incident response.

[00:08:24] Ava: what's the expected warm-up time for a new model or a rolling canary?
[00:08:29] Liam: depends on traffic and template diversity. For a medium-volume tenant, you'd see the hot templates warm in minutes; tail templates may take hours or days. We often recommend warmup jobs: replay a representative sample of prompts to pre-populate the cache. Redwood can accept bulk load transforms to seed cache entries for private deployments.

[00:08:52] [00:08:52] Priya: could you talk about observability? what signals should our SREs look at?
[00:08:58] Liam: key signals: cache hit-rate (per-tenant & global), tokens saved, avg latency delta for cached vs uncached requests, KV store memory usage by slab, eviction rate, false-positive reuse (rare), and model-variant mismatch errors. We also emit traces linking an API request to cache key used and to the backend batch that served it.

[00:09:20] Carlos: are there any heuristics you use to auto-evict or compress entries?
[00:09:25] Liam: yes. beyond LRU we have frequency-adaptive eviction — entries with low frequency and low token-savings are evicted first. For long-lived cold entries we suggest TTLs. We also can compress stored activations for less-frequent entries using lossy compression; that's tradeoff between memory and re-compute cost.

[00:09:47] Maya: on the topic of batching, how do cached prefixes affect batch composition?
[00:09:52] Liam: caching reduces decoder steps, which can change batching characteristics. If many requests are cache-hits with identical cached prefixes, they can be coalesced into the same batch and get much higher throughput. However, variance in hit/miss mixes requires the runtime to support dynamic batching. Redwood's batcher prioritizes requests by expected remaining decode length (estimated after consuming cached prefix) to keep latency SLOs.

[00:10:18] Priya: so we should expose to the batcher an estimated remaining tokens field?
[00:10:21] Liam: either estimated tokens or include a flag that prefix was fully satisfied via cache so batcher knows its short. We can infer it, but explicit hints improve scheduling.

[00:10:33] [00:10:33] Ava: any gotchas for VPC / on-prem deployments with shared NVMe or NUMA boundaries?
[00:10:39] Liam: yes hardware topology matters. On multi-socket machines you should pin cache shards to local NUMA nodes to avoid cross-socket traffic. For NVMe-backed backing stores, IO latency for cold misses can spike. For on-prem we recommend an in-memory hot slab per GPU and an NVMe cold slab, plus local SSD-backed snapshotting for fast recovery.

[00:11:05] Carlos: HSM/KMS integration — we use an HSM and cannot export keys. how does Redwood handle encryption keys for private deployments?
[00:11:12] Liam: in private deployments Redwood integrates with your KMS/HSM — keys never leave your control. Cache encryption/decryption happens on-host via KMS calls and plaintext activations never land in the control plane. We also support bring-your-own-encryption and attestations for images.

[00:11:33] Priya: ok great.

[00:11:40] Maya: quick demo idea — Liam, can you sketch the prototype we'll deliver?
[00:11:45] Liam: sure. Plan: 1) a python utility that takes your sample logs, runs template extraction & prompt fingerprinting, and outputs a list of top templates and estimated token-savings. 2) a small runtime shim we can deploy in your staging that enforces per-tenant namespace keys + demo slab config. 3) a perf harness to run 1-hour benchmark comparing baseline vs prefix-cache enabled, and produce hit-rate, tokens-saved, and latency deltas. We'll deliver step 1 by 3/17 and run step 3 with your traces by 3/18.

[00:12:19] Priya: that timeline works. we'll anonymize traces and give you tenant map.

[00:12:25] Carlos: curious about cost tradeoffs — does increased cache memory reduce compute significantly?
[00:12:30] Liam: yes, token-savings linearly reduce decoder work. For many workloads, a 30-50% reduction in token generation yields proportionate cost savings. But memory costs increase; it's a balance. Redwood Optimize can compute a projected ROI for different slab sizes.

[00:12:46] [00:12:46] Maya: any other security concerns?
[00:12:49] Ava: can we restrict which templates are shared globally? like only templates vetted by compliance?
[00:12:54] Liam: absolutely. You can whitelist or blackhole templates based on regex, or only allow global sharing for templates that pass a privacy checklist. The console supports tag-based policies to mark templates as 'private' or 'shareable'.

[00:13:08] Priya: one more question — do you support cache metrics per-customer for billing?
[00:13:13] Liam: yes, we produce per-tenant token-saved metrics which you can export to billing.

[00:13:20] Maya: wrapping up, recap: Liam will deliver the template extractor + hashing prototype by 3/17, run perf harness by 3/18 using ArgosPay traces, and we'll schedule a follow-up to review slab config and canary strategy week of 3/24. Priya will provide traces and mapping by 3/14. Ava will confirm HSM/KMS constraints by 3/19.

[00:13:45] Priya: sounds good, thanks everyone.
[00:13:50] Carlos: thanks.
[00:13:52] Liam: cool, i'll send a short doc with the hashing options (sha256 vs murmur) and tradeoffs, plus a sample normalizer.

[00:14:00] Maya: thanks all. end.

(End of transcript — timestamps are approximate; transcription contains minor mis-hearings. Reference artifacts: Liam to share prompt-fingerprint prototype repo link, Redwood console screenshots for slab config, and perf spreadsheet.)
